text: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The resolution I am putting before the House today asks the government to take immediate action to protect the health and well-being of New Brunswickers in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic. Nobody in this room needs to be reminded what that pandemic did to our communities, to our families, to our economy. The question is what we learned from it. Are we better prepared today for the next public health crisis than we were for that one? I do not believe we are, and that is why this resolution matters. The Public Health Act is the cornerstone of how this province responds to a pandemic, and it is badly in need of updating. RSV, for one — the Act needs to speak to RSV. And it needs a mechanism for adding further illnesses to the ones Public Health tracks, so that we are not back here amending the Act every time something new shows up. What we need is a system that is agile and resilient and able to respond to new and emerging threats. Getting there takes a multifaceted approach: investment in public health infrastructure, in resources, in personnel. You cannot ask a system to carry a province through a crisis if it does not have the staff or the funding to do it. We need public health education and awareness campaigns too, so that people are informed and can act to protect their own health and the health of others. And the response has to be equitable and inclusive, Mr. Speaker. Seniors, people with underlying health conditions, marginalized communities — they are hit disproportionately, every time, and the response has to be tailored to what they actually need, with the resources and supports to keep them safe and healthy. I ask all members to support this resolution. Amend the Public Health Act. Put comprehensive strategies in place. Be ready next time.

And then there is how nursing home workers were treated under Premier Higgs. He took them to court. He told them they could go to Alberta if they wanted better wages. That is not a negotiating strategy, Madam Deputy Speaker — that is a betrayal of the people who look after the most vulnerable among us. There was no empathy in it, and no thought given to the people doing that work on the front lines. Then we had the school strike. Sixteen days, and it ended with emergency orders forcing workers back on the job. What does that say about this government's commitment to real dialogue, or about the right to strike? You cannot call that a fair and balanced negotiation. Watering down binding arbitration. Scab-friendly legislation. This pension bill we are still arguing about. It is a pattern, and every piece of it chips away at workers' rights. That is not the kind of just and equitable society we say we want, one that respects the people who do the work. The decisions we make in this Chamber land on people's livelihoods and on the health of our communities, so we had better scrutinize them. Fairness. Respect. The right to bargain on an equal footing. Those are the values at stake, and the way forward is collaborative, constructive dialogue where workers actually get heard. Madam Deputy Speaker, you will remember the unions and how vehemently they disagreed with the wage-freeze mandate this government brought in — the 0% mandate, in its early years. And this was in a global pandemic, when our frontline workers were nothing short of heroes. What they gave up deserved acknowledgement and it deserved real support. As the union leaders put it, these heroes deserved more than zeroes.

of its citizens using tactics that undercut basic fairness. Taking nursing home workers to court, and then telling them to go to Alberta if they want better wages — that was regrettable, Mr. Speaker, and it told you everything about a government that had lost touch with its own people. There was a choice there. The Premier could have sat down and talked. He chose confrontation instead. Then came the offer of binding arbitration with conditions. Conditions. That was not arbitration, it was a way to cap what the workers could ask for before they ever got in the room, and it dodged the legitimate concerns those workers were bringing forward. And 10.5¢ an hour. That is what he would not go past. Ten and a half cents, for the people who look after our parents and our grandparents. That is not just unfair. It says he did not understand what those workers are worth to this province. Then, in the middle of a heated exchange with protesters, he said, "if you want that kind of wage, then Alberta's where to get it." That is dismissive, and it ignores what workers in New Brunswick are up against here at home. Rather than deal with the issue in front of him, the Premier deflected. His responsibility is to the people of New Brunswick, and we will remind him of that as many times as it takes. He also claimed that fair wages would not fix the staffing shortages in our nursing homes. He is wrong. A fair wage is justice for the worker, yes, and it is also how you recruit and keep people in these jobs. The Premier did not treat this as urgent and he did not sit down with those workers in any meaningful way.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate two authors from L'nui Menikuk, also known as Indian Island First Nation. Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck have put out a cookbook called Mitji — Let's Eat!: Mi'kmaq Recipes from Sikniktuk. Mr. Speaker, calling it a cookbook undersells it. The recipes come with the history and the lived experience of a community that has been on these lands for generations, and that is the part that stays with you when you read it. The two of them also take on gastrocolonialism, which is the way colonial policy went into Indigenous kitchens and changed traditional recipes. That is not a small thing to write about, and they wrote about it well. The people of Mi'gma'gi have a rich heritage and a resilient spirit, and this book carries both. I would ask all members to join me in congratulating Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck for the work they are doing to keep Indigenous culinary traditions alive.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I want to talk about labour relations in this province, because I do not think we are in a good place on it. Workers need it to work. So does the economy. What we have seen from the Higgs government over the last few years is a pattern, and it is not a good one. When there is a labour issue, this government does not go to the table. It comes in here and passes a law. Bill 23 in 2022. Bill 17 last fall. The essential service legislation we debated back in December 2019. Three times, Mr. Speaker. Three separate occasions where the choice was made to legislate inside this Chamber instead of sitting down with workers and their representatives and working it out. Do that without proper consultation and you get exactly what we have got — more tension, and a wider gap between the government and the people who do the work. The amendments to the Public Service Labour Relations Act. The change to the essential service legislation, which was controversial and everybody knew it was going to be. Every one of those was a chance to build some trust with the labour movement, and every one of those chances went by. What you build instead is the opposite of trust, and you cannot run a workplace without it. People feel it out there. Workers are discouraged. Morale is down. That shows up in what our industries produce and in how people are doing, and the whole province wears it.

Mr. Speaker, the strain on labour relations in this province is not something anybody can pretend away anymore. It is hanging over every effort we make together to build prosperity in New Brunswick. And if we are going to deal with it honestly, we have to admit that the legislative approach this government took has fallen short. Going forward, it has to be real dialogue, it has to be transparency, and it has to be respect both ways when we sit down with workers and the people who represent them. Trust is the thing. Build that, and everybody's interests get taken seriously. Skip it, and they do not.

Go back to December 2019, Mr. Speaker. This Legislature was in the middle of a very ugly debate over the essential service legislation, and what it came down to was the wages of nursing home workers. Bill 17. That bill put conditions on how labour arbitrators could rule on those wages. The reaction was intense. Members of the New Brunswick Council of Nursing Home Unions came out against it. They were worried about what it would do to their ability to strike and to bargain a fair wage, and they said so loudly. Nobody was in any doubt about how deep that discontent ran.

The bill passed anyway. Union leaders called it what they thought it was — an attack on public-sector labour unions. Sharon Teare, President of the New Brunswick Council of Nursing Home Unions, said their voice would not be silenced. She meant it. They kept fighting for better working conditions and for the rights of nursing home workers, and those workers do valuable work in this society.

Bill 17 showed the tension between this government and labour, especially around labour rights and collective bargaining. It is not a simple balance. Workers on one side, taxpayers and the government's fiscal responsibility on the other. But when we look back at December 2019 and that bill, let us not forget that there are people sitting in government right now who opposed it. They said so out loud. They said they would stand with the labour movement as long as they could. That has changed today.

Madam Speaker, let me walk members through what this one does. Right now the Act says you cannot have quorum for the executive committee unless a particular deputy head is in the room — the deputy head whose mandate has a direct impact on the economy — or their delegate. And here is the wrinkle. That individual does not even vote. The structure was put in there to keep economic alignment right across government, which is a fine goal. What has happened in practice is scheduling headaches, and decisions sitting and waiting because the required deputy head could not be there. The amendment before us is straightforward. Change the quorum requirement so that a simple majority of the voting members present is quorum for the executive committee. That is already how it works for the board of directors. We made a similar amendment to this Act in 2021 to simplify the board's definition of quorum, so this makes the two consistent. I should note what is not changing. The composition of the executive committee stays the same. So does the participation of the deputy head whose mandate has a direct impact on the economy. That person is a valued contributor to the committee's work and remains one. All this does is let the committee meet and conduct its business without unnecessary disruption. In a fast-paced economic environment, being able to act swiftly and effectively is essential. Streamline the quorum requirement and Opportunities New Brunswick is better positioned to deliver programs, to respond to emerging opportunities, and to support the businesses that drive growth in our province. It is a small, practical piece of legislation, Madam Speaker, the kind that keeps an agency working. Administrative, yes. But it will have a meaningful benefit for operational continuity. I encourage all members to support this amendment to the Opportunities New Brunswick Act. A modest step, and an important one, so that Opportunities New Brunswick can keep fulfilling its mandate — growth, investment and opportunity for all New Brunswickers. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, on November 11 we stop and we remember. We remember the men and women who served this country in war, in conflict and in peacekeeping, and the ones who are still serving today. Their courage, their sacrifice, their sense of duty — that is what kept the freedom and the values we have now. We remember the families too, the ones who carried the separation and carried the grief. We remember the veterans who came home changed by what they did. I will say that again, Madam Speaker, because it matters: the families who carried the burden of separation and loss, and the veterans who came home forever changed by their service. When we gather at the cenotaphs and the memorials across New Brunswick this year, let us renew the commitment. To peace. To gratitude. To never forgetting the ones who gave everything for Canada. Lest we forget. Lest we forget.

I want to start with the good in this bill, because there is some. It clears out language that should have gone years ago and puts plain English where the legal Latin used to be. That sounds like housekeeping, but clarity matters. It also makes it simpler for brewers and distillers to sell at approved farmers' markets, which is something our small producers here have been asking for a long time. A microbrewery or a craft distillery being able to stand at the Saint Andrews farmers' market, or the St. George market, or the market in St. Stephen, and sell to a customer face to face — that brings tourists in, it encourages people to start something of their own, and the money stays local. I applaud that part of the bill, Madam Speaker. The sector has taken off in this province and the bill recognizes it. Modernizing is fine. Modernizing without scrutiny is not. The bill sets production caps: 500 000 L for brewers and 75 000 L for distillers, when they are operating as agents under the New Brunswick Liquor Corporation. On the face of it those look like fair numbers. Who were they worked out with, though? Our smaller producers, or mainly the larger operators? And does a cap set at that level end up favouring the people already established, so a start-up has a harder time growing into the next tier? We have watched this happen before. A well-intentioned regulatory change turns out to suit the outfits with deeper pockets and more connections, while the small owner is dealing with compliance costs and waiting on a licence. Craft producers in St. Croix and elsewhere put their life savings into a brewery or a distillery, and what they say to me is simple enough: we do not mind rules, we just want fair ones. So my question to the government is this. How will fairness between small and large producers be ensured under this new licencing model?

Picture a family. Nothing unusual about them. A quiet town, could be yours, could be mine. Their boy is bright, doing well, everything ahead of him. Then he gets hurt — an injury, or surgery, and there is a prescription for the pain, and that is where it starts. The pills stop being medicine after a while. They become a crutch. Then a necessity. Then the whole of it. I will call him Alex. School goes first, then the friendships, then whatever he used to think of himself. One day he is gone. Left home. He is out at the encampments on the edge of town, the ones in the woods, under the bridges, on lots nobody has used in twenty years, where getting through the day means finding the next fix. Now think about his mother and father. They are wrecked, and they go out anyway, every day, without fail. They bring sandwiches, fruit, water. They bring clean clothes — jackets, socks, blankets, because the nights are cold. They walk in among the tents and the clusters of people and they call his name. Alex, it is Mom and Dad. We are here for you. They look at every face for something they recognize. Nobody answers. Not that day, not the next one. They show his picture to strangers and ask if anyone has seen him. Weeks of that, then months of it. They do not sleep. Is he safe. Is he alive. Has it taken him already. They hold on to each other and keep going. They know what the numbers say about overdoses, about the people who do not come back. They hold on to hope anyway. It is the only thing they have got.

Madam Speaker, let me be clear on what this bill does. It makes things easier. It does not approve anything. It takes barriers out of the way, it adds clarity, and it puts New Brunswick in a position to move when the time comes. The proposal was drafted with several departments at the table — the Office of the Attorney General, Service New Brunswick, the Department of Post-Secondary Education, Training and Labour, and the Department of Indigenous Affairs. The NB Power Board of Directors will go on overseeing all security measures, so the financial accountability and the risk mitigation stay where they are. The information gathered becomes the basis of the proposal that goes to government for approval, and it gets reviewed before any authorization is given. Madam Speaker, the Mactaquac Life Achievement Project is a bold investment in our energy future, and a necessary one. This bill makes sure we are ready for what it brings, with the flexibility and the clarity and the confidence that will be required. I will say that again, because it is the heart of it: this legislation is what gets us ready. I would urge all members to support the bill and help us take the next step toward securing clean energy for New Brunswickers, today and for decades to come. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. We have guests with us this afternoon — members of the New Brunswick Psychiatric Association are in the gallery, and I believe the association's Board of Directors is up there as well. I'd ask members to give them a welcome. These are dedicated professionals, and the work they do supporting New Brunswickers' mental health and well-being is essential. I'll say as well that the association keeps working closely with the Department of Health, and that collaboration is doing a lot to strengthen our system of care. I'll have more to say about that later on today. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, we have a new provincial website up, and I am glad to tell the House about it. It is artsculturenb.ca. The point of it is to get more people paying attention to the arts, culture and creative industries in this province, and it is up just in time for the holidays. What you will find there are artists, artisans and cultural experiences from all over New Brunswick. If you are looking for a gift that is a bit different, or an event or a performance to go to, that is where to look. And it works the other way too. If you are in the arts and culture sector, there is a place on that site to upload your own events and your own work and get it in front of people. So go to artsculturenb.ca and have a look at what is being made in this province. Shop local this season. Celebrate our own talent. Support the artists who make this place extraordinary. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, today is the International Day of Persons with Disabilities. I want to recognize the strength, the contributions, and the resilience of persons with disabilities right across New Brunswick. Our commitment is to a province where every person has an equal opportunity to take part fully — in our communities, in our schools, in our workplaces, in our public spaces. We showed what that commitment looks like this summer. We made sure the federal Canada Disability Benefit would not detract from provincial disability programs, because federal programs should complement provincial support, not replace it. Madam Speaker, a day like today is a reminder that accessibility and inclusion are not optional. Without them there is no real equity. So let us keep at it together — removing barriers, promoting dignity, and making sure every New Brunswicker can live, work, and thrive without limitations. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, on October 24, Ms. Laura Anderson of Newtown turned 105. One hundred and five. She is still living independently, in her own home, and she is as sharp and as strong as anybody I know. Up until last month she still had her driver's licence, and she used it — short drives on the rural roads out there, roads she has known her whole life. Laura and her late husband, Thomas, did a lot for this province. They were founding members of the Agricultural Museum of New Brunswick, so a good part of our farming heritage is preserved because those two thought it was worth preserving. In 1967, they started the first farm vacation in New Brunswick. Families came from all over the province, and travellers came from around the world. She still tells the stories, Mr. Speaker, and she still has the humour to go with them. One hundred and five remarkable years. We congratulate her, and we thank her for everything she has given this province.

Madam Speaker, our government presented the 2026-27 capital budget. It's $1.47 billion. That's $200 million above last year, and it's the biggest capital budget this province has ever seen. The bulk of it is going to the Department of Transportation and Infrastructure, for our roads, our bridges, our ferries and the rest of the essential infrastructure out there. Health care sees significant investment too — modernizing medical equipment, renovating hospitals. In education, we're building new schools in Shediac and in Moncton, and upgrading several institutions elsewhere in the province. Madam Speaker, none of this is optional. There's a backlog, and it built up over years of underinvestment, and somebody has to work through it. These investments show where our commitment is: on safety, on quality of life, and on the future of our communities for the generations coming after us. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, when somebody walks through a door looking for help, they should not have to find out that mental health is one door and addiction is another one down the hall. Those two things travel together far more often than not. So we are building a system where the two work hand in hand and are dealt with together.

What integrating the services buys you is a continuum that actually holds. Prevention, treatment, recovery, harm reduction, all of it connected, so people can get the right supports at every stage of the journey rather than falling through the cracks between programs.

For children and youth, the work starts early and it happens in the community. Get in early and substance use does not escalate, and the long-term harms come down.

For someone already living with addiction, it is about getting them in the door in time and having something real on the other side of it. Detox services. Live-in programs. Outpatient counselling. Long-term recovery supports. A full range, not one option.

The investments back that up. We launched the Moncton Addictions and Mental Health Court. When a person with mental health and addiction challenges comes into contact with the justice system, that court gives them a chance at treatment and community supports instead. If they are facing criminal charges, it is an alternative pathway to traditional sentencing, connecting them to treatment and recovery. It eases pressure on the justice system too, and participants do better over the long term.

And this week we announced a new 50-bed addiction treatment facility — a first step on treatment capacity, and we are actively exploring more beds across New Brunswick.

Beds need staff. That is why the workforce piece is in here, including ten newly established trainer positions to build skills, expertise and resilience in the addictions and mental health workforce.

All of it together, Madam Speaker, means stronger service delivery, consistency across the province, and people living with substance use challenges getting the right care at the right time and in the right setting.

Madam Speaker, if there are seniors watching this morning in the Miramichi area, here is something worth knowing about. Nursing Home Without Walls is at the Miramichi Regional Hospital today, in the main lobby, from 7 a.m. until 2 p.m. They are there with Horizon Health Network to sit down with people and get them set up on MyHealthNB. That is the secure portal where you can look at your own blood work and your own imaging results. You need two things: a Medicare card and an email address. That is it. Horizon staff will check your identity right there and hand you the access code on the spot. No appointment. Nobody has to register ahead of time. This is the sort of thing Nursing Home Without Walls does well, Madam Speaker — taking a barrier away so seniors can stay on top of their own health information and stay independent. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. A sad one today. Robert Hosford passed away on Wednesday, November 12. Husband, father, uncle, great-uncle, pop pop to his grandchildren, and a friend to more people than I could name here. Robert was the cornerstone of that family. Their needs came first, his came second, and that was how he wanted it. A helping hand or a listening ear — whichever you needed, that is what you got. His laugh was the kind you could hear across a room, Madam Speaker, and his humour could turn a tough day into one you ended up telling people about. He cheered for his family louder than he cheered for anybody, and he cheered pretty loud at a ball game. Sports and family, that was Robert, and family always won. He leaves behind love, laughter and adventure. To his family and to his friends, our condolences. Thank you.

Madam Speaker, a new family health team was announced in Bathurst yesterday, and I am glad to be able to stand up and say so. This clinic is one of a number opening across New Brunswick right now. That is what a movement looks like when it starts to take hold — community clinics opening up, more people getting in the door for primary care, and families having a place to go where the care carries on from one visit to the next. For people in our region this is a real change, Madam Speaker. More professionals under one roof. Intake that is more flexible. And when you need to be sent somewhere else, you get sent to the right place. That collaborative model is slowly changing how care gets delivered in this province, and it is built on three things: being close to where people live, keeping people well in the first place, and having the different professions work together. Every opening is us doing what we said we would do. In Bathurst and in other places too, the progress is very real. Promise made, promise kept, Madam Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, New Brunswickers are going to be gathered around the Christmas tree in a couple of weeks, and they will be exchanging more than presents. They will be exchanging stories about how this Holt government turned its promises into ornaments. Sparkly. Shiny. Hollow. The balanced budget was going to come with fanfare and a drumroll, we were told. What is under the tree instead? A deficit. Not the gift that keeps on giving, Mr. Speaker. The gift that keeps on taking. And the carbon tax adjustor. That was a promise you could have kept with the stroke of a pen. Still there. Still adding to the price of everything people buy every single day. That is not the Christmas cheer we were hoping for. There have been a lot of promises made to New Brunswickers. This government needs to figure out that promises are not just for the Christmas season. They are for the rest of the year too. Deliver.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the minister's statement on the InnovateNB Awards, and I want to say up front that the recipients deserve every bit of it. These are people doing hard things in a small province. Good on them. Now, having said that, celebrating is the easy part. Innovation does not exist in a vacuum. It needs a support system around it, and we still have barriers in New Brunswick that plenty of innovators hit head-on. The minister spoke about a growing confidence in the business climate here. I would ask, confidence for whom? Because it is not evenly spread across sectors and it is certainly not evenly spread across communities. Our rural areas still struggle to get at the resources and the supports that the urban centres take for granted. That is the part I keep hearing about back home. If the benefits of innovation reach only the people who already have the networks, then this is not a provincial strategy, it is a strategy for a couple of postal codes. And what about the next crowd coming up? That is the question nobody puts on the awards program. Cultivating the next generation of innovators means investing in education, it means mentorship, and it means funds that are actually accessible to somebody without a lawyer. Our young people should be leading this, not watching it. Research and development is the other thing. We celebrate results while the investment that produces results goes short, especially in the sectors we say we are betting on, clean technology and sustainable practices. So my ask is simple. Let us work at this together, government and industry and communities, and build something inclusive enough that innovation is open to every New Brunswicker. Our future depends on it. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. With the holidays coming, I want to say a word about shopping local. Small business is the heartbeat of the economy in this province. It is the cafe and the restaurant where people meet up. It is the boutique and the artisan that give a downtown its character. It is the family shop that has been handed from one generation to the next, and the local producer turning out work that is world class right here at home. Those are not just storefronts, Madam Speaker. They are employers. They support the minor hockey team. They are a big part of how our regions grow. When you shop local at Christmas you are not just buying a gift. More of that dollar stays in New Brunswick. It goes into jobs, into local suppliers, into the economies of our own regions. That is a ripple, and it is a powerful one. It is what lets a small business grow and keep serving the community it cares about. I was at the Premier's open house yesterday. The turnout was strong and the range of vendors there was something to see. New Brunswickers want to buy local, and the talent in our small business community is remarkable. So get out to the markets this season. Go into the neighbourhood shops. Find the artisans. Choose New Brunswick-made products and services. Big choices, small choices — they add up, and they add up most at this time of year. When you shop local you are supporting the people who support all of us the rest of the year. One more word on the open house. It was exciting to see such a diverse range of folks. I talked to one vendor who started his business when he was nine years old. Nine. WHEREAS the From Surfaces to Services report came out in 2017, and it said we needed one comprehensive, coordinated approach to public transportation in this province, and since then nothing meaningful has been done; WHEREAS putting a Minister in charge of public transportation would give us the leadership, the coordination and the accountability we need to actually develop, fund and connect these services across New Brunswick; BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that this Legislative Assembly urge the Premier to give the Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure a mandate for public transportation; BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that this Legislative Assembly urge the government to put the resources and the funding behind the New Brunswick Transportation Authority so it can create a public transportation strategy and carry it out.

What we heard, too often, is that the subsidies and the economic development incentives go to the big corporations, and not to the small and medium-sized businesses that create most of the local jobs in our communities. Point that investment at the smaller operators and you strengthen the local economy, and the wealth that gets generated by that activity stays here in New Brunswick communities. One idea that came up, and I think it is a good one, is stronger support for community economic development corporations. Those let residents put money directly into a business by buying community investment shares. Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island have run similar models and have launched hundreds of enterprises off the back of them — renewable energy projects, community ventures, that sort of thing. Given proper provincial support, and some promotion, this could be a real driver of local entrepreneurship and resilience here. Citizens also had a lot to say about the energy strategy and the need to modernize it. Instead of leaning so heavily on the large, high-risk megaprojects, there is growing support for diversifying, with the focus on efficiency and on renewables. Some of what was put forward: an energy investment fund to get new technologies to commercialization, a modest levy on electrical bills dedicated to efficiency and renewable projects, and a Property Assessed Clean Energy program to pay for solar, battery storage and efficiency upgrades. Do those things and you bring household energy costs down, you create skilled jobs, and you start dealing with the long-term electrical demand problem that NB Power is looking at. The last one is procurement. Citizens want the province to use its purchasing power for local economies. Government spends tens of millions of dollars a year on goods and services, and a lot of that money goes to large corporations or to suppliers outside the province. Redirect even a small part of it to local businesses, cooperatives and social enterprises, and you create real opportunity in communities across New Brunswick. The hospitals, the universities, the schools, the correctional facilities — those institutions know what they need to buy and they buy it every year. Aim even a small share of those contracts at local suppliers on purpose and the benefit ripples right across the province.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I was very sorry to hear of the passing of Hon. Mark McLane, Prince Edward Island's Minister of Health and Wellness. He gave a great deal to public service, and the work he did to improve the lives of Islanders is going to outlast him. In government he was a person of integrity. He was compassionate, and he genuinely wanted a stronger health system and a stronger community. What he did in public office, and outside of it, will be remembered and appreciated for a long time to come. To Mark's family, to his friends and colleagues, and to all Islanders who felt the effect of his work and his leadership, my heartfelt condolences. He will be greatly missed. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, the month of March gives us a chance to pay tribute to social workers, and their work matters a great deal in the lives of New Brunswickers. They offer care, they advocate, and they support people, and they do all of it with empathy and respect. For a lot of families, a social worker is where healing starts. Where resilience comes from. Where hope comes from. They transform lives, Madam Speaker, and they uplift communities, and what drives them is a commitment to dignity and human rights. Their roles are all over the place, and I mean that as a compliment: addictions and mental health, children and youth in care, seniors, women and gender equity. Within the Department of Social Development we have over 600 social workers. They help New Brunswickers access long-term care and disability support. They help protect children and seniors from abuse. They support foster families. They advocate for vulnerable individuals and they make sure vital services reach the people in need of them. This National Social Work Month, we thank them for their compassion, their resilience, and their commitment to improving lives and to building stronger communities across New Brunswick. Their dedication does not waver, and it makes a lasting difference every day. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, let me go through how it works. An employee has to have 90 days of continuous employment before they are eligible for the leave. That is the same threshold other provinces use. The employee has to tell the employer as soon as they can that they need it. And an employer can ask for reasonable medical documentation showing the person is not able to work because of illness or injury. None of that is unusual. It keeps the leave honest and it gives employers some assurance and some predictability about what is coming. Madam Speaker, this is a step forward. It gives workers protection at the point where they are most vulnerable, and it does it in a way that takes account of what workplaces across this province actually look like. It goes to something bigger too, which is whether New Brunswick is a place where a person can live and work with dignity. Nobody should have to pick between their health and their job. Right now our legislation leaves a gap there. This amendment fills it. It protects people while they are sick and it keeps the process reasonable and structured for the employer. It is practical, it is needed, and it is the sort of balance we ought to be aiming for in our labour standards. Thank you very much, Madam Speaker. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I rise today about the Battle of Vimy Ridge, fought on April 9, 1917, and about why it still matters. It is one of the defining moments in Canada's history. The Vimy Foundation has been at this since 2006, raising awareness and teaching Canadians about the battle, and this year's campaign begins the lead-up to the 110th anniversary in 2027. That is going to be a milestone moment for this country. Vimy Week is April 2 to 9, and I'd ask all members of this House to wear the Vimy Pin. If you look closely at it, there are four distinct colours, and they're there for the four Canadian divisions that fought together for the first time at Vimy Ridge. Unity and sacrifice, that's what the pin is saying. When we wear it we honour their courage, their sacrifice and the legacy they left behind, and that legacy helped define our nation. Thank you, Madam Speaker

Madam Speaker, we're coming up on a year since our government launched the universal breakfast program in every school in New Brunswick. That was last September. The results are already showing. Every morning, right across the province, kids are sitting down to milk, eggs, bagels, apples and cheese before the bell goes. We work with FeedNB on this, and that partnership is what lets schools put healthy food on the table — a lot of it coming off our own farms and out of our own local businesses. For a lot of families this matters, Madam Speaker, and it matters more with what groceries cost now. It saves parents money. It saves them time. It takes some of the pressure out of a weekday morning, and anybody with young kids at home knows what those mornings are like. And the kids get to class fed, so they can actually concentrate and take part in the day. That is a real investment in these young people. Every child should get to start the day on the right foot. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I rise today a happy man, and a grateful one. People in my part of the province have been waiting on this for years, and the new bridge between Île Lamèque and Shippagan, the one we have hoped for all that time, is going to be built. My thanks to the Premier, Hon. Susan Holt, and to the Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure, Hon. Chuck Chiasson, who came out to the region in February to make the announcement in person. That marks a turning point for our communities. It will simplify travel for people, it will strengthen our connections with the rest of the province, and it will bring new economic opportunities our way. On behalf of my constituents, I want to say thank you to everyone who played a part in making this project happen for our community. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I want to tell the House about Charlie Burrell. Charlie is proof of what one person can do in a community. Out in Little River he has put his own time and his own energy into building a facility and small homes for people who are homeless — people most of us walk past and forget about. He saw his friends, and that is what he calls them, his friends, living on the streets of Moncton. He could have turned away. He did not. He stepped up. He brings them food and clothing, and that matters, but what matters more is that he gives them dignity and he gives them hope. Charlie reminds us that homelessness is not an issue. It is a human being having a hard time, and everyone deserves kindness and a chance. His work has pulled that community together and it has got other people involved. Change starts with one person deciding to care. Thank you, Charlie. You care so much.

Madam Speaker, I was sad to learn that Roméo H. LeBlanc has passed away at the age of 102. He was an Acadian, and he served in the Second World War. As Minister responsible for Military Affairs, I want to take a moment for him here today. His service to this country was exceptional. But it did not stop when the war stopped. He spent the rest of his life looking after other veterans and making sure the people who served were not forgotten. Courage, devotion, a sense of duty — that was Mr. LeBlanc, right through to 102 years of age, and young people coming up behind him will have something to look to in that. On behalf of the government of New Brunswick, my condolences to his family, to those close to him, and to the whole veterans' community. We will remember him. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

As the province modernizes its assessment system, the rationale for a separate assessment fee gets thinner. Modern assessment relies on digital tools. Automated evaluation models. Data pulled in from several sources. Less manual work. When that is how the system operates, the cost of assessment belongs where every other core function of government belongs, in the budget, not tacked onto a bill. Eliminating the fee reflects the modernization we say we are doing. It would also support rural and small-community residents. Out there you find lower incomes, higher transportation costs, fewer local services, and limited access to affordable housing. The fee is felt more acutely in those communities. Getting rid of it would be a meaningful gesture toward rural New Brunswickers, many of whom have made their frustration with the property tax system very clear. And it is a source of public backlash year after year. Property tax bills go out, and the assessment fee is the thing people latch onto. That erodes trust. It distracts from broader reform. It undermines confidence. Eliminating the fee removes a flashpoint we know is coming every twelve months. Eliminating the assessment fee on the 484 000 property tax bills issued in New Brunswick is a practical and timely measure, and it aligns with the province's own stated goals for property tax reform. It would improve affordability, rebuild public trust, simplify administration, support rural and low-income residents, reinforce the assessment freeze, align with modernization efforts and demonstrate that somebody here is listening. Here is the part that should trouble members. Based on the best available public reporting, the assessment fee generates millions of dollars per year, and the government of New Brunswick has not publicly disclosed the exact total. The fee is set at $19.40 per $100 000 of assessed value. The total revenue therefore depends entirely on the combined provincial assessment base. The legislation applies $19.40 per $100 000 of assessed value to every property tax bill in the province, and because assessments have risen sharply in recent years, the fee is growing rapidly. The province does not publish a line-item total in its budget documents. No public source provides an official aggregate revenue figure. So what can we infer from the structure of the fee?

Thank you, Madam Speaker. Our government's economic development strategy comes down to one priority. Build a stronger, more competitive New Brunswick, and make it a place where people here find opportunity. This province succeeds when our businesses succeed. A company that grows, that gets into new markets, that puts money back into its own operations, is a company that hires people. That is what holds communities together and that is what pays for the public services families count on every single day. The strategy is built on the strengths we already have. It is about productivity, about supporting innovation, and about helping New Brunswick companies compete and succeed in a global economy that does not sit still. It also holds us to what we said on attracting investment and on strengthening key sectors, defence and mining among them, and on growth that lasts. The approach is coordinated and it is accountable. Departments are working to the same priorities and to outcomes we can measure. Government cannot do this on its own. It takes alignment inside government and real collaboration with industry, with academia, with communities across the province, and with the members of this House. The early feedback from stakeholders has been positive, and what they point to is the clarity, the discipline and the results focus. New Brunswick has what the world wants. We are competing to win, and we are setting the conditions for businesses to grow, communities to thrive and opportunity to spread across this province. When the economy grows, the services get better and the future gets better for all New Brunswickers. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Bill 40 makes some significant amendments to the Health Quality and Patient Safety Act. That Act already exists, and it already sets up a framework for reviewing patient safety incidents and learning from them. The government says the amendments will improve how health care incidents are reviewed, strengthen collaboration, make things more consistent and give patients and families more transparency. Fine. Nobody is going to stand up and argue against a system that learns better and communicates better. But we do not judge legislation by what it intends. We judge it by what it does, and reading Bill 40 closely raises questions. The first one is basic. Before we build new structures or hand out new powers, what is the specific problem here? The Act already provides a framework for patient safety reviews. So what failed? Are reviews not happening? Are the lessons not being shared? Are patients being left in the dark? Are the health authorities ignoring the recommendations they get? Those concerns came up at the briefing on the bill, and rightly so. Legislative change should follow a demonstrated gap, and the government has not put forward clear data showing a systemic failure under the current law. Without that, we are legislating in search of a problem instead of solving one. Diagnosis comes before treatment. That is true in a hospital and it is true in here. Then there is the biggest change in the bill, the creation of a New Brunswick Quality of Care and Patient Safety Advisory Committee, established and maintained by the minister. On paper it sounds reasonable enough. Who is against expert advice on patient safety? This is where I would ask members to slow down. Health care professionals in this province already work inside a stack of oversight structures. Horizon. Vitalité. The professional regulatory colleges. Accreditation bodies. Internal quality review committees. Patient advocacy offices. So which is this, better outcomes or more bureaucracy? Front-line workers are already telling us they spend more and more of their day filling out forms instead of caring for patients. If this committee turns into one more reporting layer and no measurable improvement comes of it, we will have made the very system we set out to fix worse.

The bill lets the minister require health care organizations to put improvement plans in place. Fine. Accountability matters. But there is a risk on the other side of that, and it is centralization. These organizations are not operating in the same world as one another. An urban hospital is not a rural facility. A community clinic is not a long-term care home. Something designed at the centre and applied to all of them may not fit what any of them are actually dealing with. Ministerial authority should be supporting improvement, not standing in for professional judgment. Oversight guides. It does not micromanage. The part of this bill that worries me most is subsection 6.2. It says that where the Health Quality and Patient Safety Act conflicts with the Right to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, this Act wins. That is a big legal step, and members opposite should say so plainly. They are carving an exception out of one of the core privacy protections we have over public institutions. Now, the government's argument is that confidentiality keeps the discussion open during safety reviews. There is something to that. A health care professional has to be able to speak candidly and not worry about it. But overriding privacy legislation that is already on the books demands rigorous justification. What information gets withheld? Withheld from whom? Under what safeguards? And if you are refused, what is your appeal? Transparency and confidentiality have to be balanced here. Too much secrecy and the public stops trusting the system. Too little and nobody reports honestly. Committee needs to go through this clause line by line. The bill also expands the rules to allow disclosure of incident reports and improvement findings. System-wide learning is a good objective. But whatever disclosure framework comes out of this has to protect patient identity while still letting the institution learn. And here is the thing I keep coming back to: information cannot just flow upward into the bureaucracy and stop there. It has to reach the front-line practitioner who is in a position to prevent that from happening again. Learning has to travel horizontally across the system, not just vertically into a report. One theme runs all the way through this bill, and that is administration. New committees. New reporting obligations. New procedural requirements. Administration is not a bad word. But a health care system only works when the administration you add is matched by clinical benefit. An hour spent writing a report is an hour not spent with a patient. The government needs to show us that all of this will measurably improve care outcomes. If it cannot, we are adding weight to a system that is already strained.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. On the bill dealing with long-term illness and injury leave. It protects workers, and I think it is essential. Nobody should have to choose between their health and their financial security when life turns difficult on them, and this bill recognizes that. Again, Madam Speaker, this is not an ordinary bill. It is a concrete commitment to the dignity, security and well-being of our people. Twenty-seven weeks of protected leave at the outside, and the guarantee that a person returns to their position or an equivalent one. That is stability for workers. It is stability for their families too. Compassion, equity, social justice — those are the values behind it. It updates our employment standards and it gives a better balance between human realities and professional responsibilities. Madam Speaker, what our legislative initiatives are for is to support people through vulnerability, suffering and injustice. They are not just housekeeping measures.

Madam Speaker, the cost of assessment fee shows up on the property tax bill and it goes to Finance and Treasury Board. Fine. But that is not the only place the homeowner pays. The local tax rate takes care of the rest, because municipalities turn around and pay Service New Brunswick for assessment services. Same property owner, two payments. One you can see and one you cannot.

I have had people at the door look at that bill and say, well, at least I know what assessment costs me. No, you do not. What is printed there is one half of it. The municipal side never shows up on your bill at all.

Now, I want to say something plainly. Nothing in this motion is a shot at Service New Brunswick. Their work is not the problem. We need assessments and municipalities need them done properly. Service New Brunswick delivers an actual service to municipalities and to rural districts, and I am not going to stand here and pretend otherwise.

What is Finance and Treasury Board delivering? Not assessment services. It is a charge on a tax bill, collected. That is it. That is the charge the motion would get rid of. After years of assessments climbing and costs climbing, it is past time.

And there is a feeling out there, Madam Speaker, that government comes out ahead on things ordinary people have no say over. Who asked for property values to jump? Not one homeowner. Not one senior on a fixed income asked to have a modest house reassessed way up. Assessments have gone up in recent years. Everybody in this room knows it. COVID hit, people moved to New Brunswick, prices went up. Fair market value drives a lot of the assessment process, and that is where the increase came from. Assessments rise, and the revenue off this fee rises right along with them. That perception is a troubling one. It looks like government benefits from the very increases that are causing stress and anxiety for the people paying the bill.

What this approach allows us to do, then, is refocus public resources on their core mission while using the expertise of the private sector for routine care. The goal here isn't to withdraw. The goal is a more modern, sustainable model, one that's aligned with Canadian best practices, so we can be sure of robust veterinary services that fit the challenges we have today and the ones we'll have tomorrow. Done right, modernization lets New Brunswick build a model around the specific needs of farms without giving up on quality. Let me turn to the concerns, because the government recognizes that bringing in this new system is causing some. For remote regions, the questions are about the quality of the services and about the cost. And in a number of those regions, access is already a considerable challenge as it stands. So a support program for private sector veterinarians is being developed. One objective of that program is to offset certain costs — travel expenses, for instance — so that producers in all regions can keep getting the services they need. Have the responses we've given cleared up every worry? No, they haven't. But they do underscore a commitment to concrete solutions tailored to each situation. Now, laboratory services. They're a key part of this transition, and they'll be essential for the early detection of emerging diseases, the prevention of health crises, and food safety. During the transition, the existing laboratories remain fully operational, so the work of farmers and veterinarians is not disrupted. Given the scale of the change, we need consensus around the proposed solutions, and we're still open to your opinions, your ideas and your worries. Together we can perfect a system that's balanced in quality and in cost, that protects farming families, and that holds up over the long term. The new model rests on a significant transformation, and how well it works will depend in large part on active cooperation, on commitment, and on a willingness to take part in the transition with an open mind.
